chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refractive index from an oblique ray
question: Light travels from air into glass. A ray is incident at 60^° and refracts at 35^°. Calculate the refractive index of the glass relative to air.
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 170" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 82 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="10" y="84" width="300" height="76" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M160 10 V160" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.2" /><path d="M48 18 L160 82 L204 160" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><text x="18" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="18" y="103" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Glass</text><text x="95" y="42" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">i = 60°</text><text x="169" y="124" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">r = 35°</text></svg>
explanation:
Using Snell's law,


n=(sin i / sin r)
=(sin60^° / sin35^°)



n=(0.8660 / 0.5736)≈1.51


Option A results from using an incorrect trigonometric ratio. Option D overestimates the ratio.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Calculating lateral displacement through a glass slab
question: A ray passes through a parallel-sided glass slab of thickness 4 cm. The angle of incidence is 60^°, and the angle of refraction is 30^°. Calculate the lateral displacement.
explanation:
For a parallel-sided slab,


d=t(sin(i-r) / cos r)


Substituting,


d=4(sin30^° / cos30^°)



d=4(0.5 / 0.8660)
≈2.31 cm


**Correction:** The calculated answer is 2.31 cm, so **D is the correct answer**. Option B incorrectly uses a different trigonometric ratio.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Finding the real depth of a glass block containing an air bubble
question: An air bubble appears 5 cm below the top surface of a glass block when viewed vertically from air. The refractive index of glass is 1.5. Calculate the real depth of the bubble.

options.text: 5.0 cm
6.5 cm
7.5 cm

explanation:
For an object inside glass viewed from air,


n=frac{d_{real}}{d_{apparent}}


Therefore,


d_{real}=1.5×5=7.5 cm


Option A incorrectly divides the apparent depth by the refractive index.

title: Identifying the correct refracted ray
question: Air above the horizontal boundary; glass below it. The normal is vertical at the point of incidence. A light ray travels from air into glass. Four candidate rays are shown in the figure. Which candidate correctly represents the refracted ray if the incident angle is 50^° and the refractive index of glass is 1.5?
diagramSvg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 190" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#f8fafc; border-radius:8px; border:1px solid #cbd5e1; font-family:system-ui, sans-serif;"><text x="230" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0f172a">HOTS Analytical Diagram: Identifying the correct refracted ray</text><rect x="40" y="45" width="380" height="95" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#cbd5e1"/><text x="230" y="72" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#1e40af">High Order Thinking Principles</text><text x="230" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#334155">Refer to the experimental variables and quantitative relationships in the problem</text><text x="230" y="114" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" font-weight="600" fill="#16a34a">Rigorous ICSE Class 10 Syllabus Correlation</text><text x="230" y="165" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" font-weight="600" fill="#64748b">Standard Analytical Schema</text></svg>

options.text: A ray in glass making an angle of approximately 75^° with the normal.
A ray in glass making an angle of approximately 30.7^° with the normal.
A ray in glass making an angle of 50^° with the normal.
A ray in glass making an angle of approximately 59.3^° with the normal.

explanation:
By Snell’s law,


n=(sin i / sin r)


Taking the refractive index of air as 1,


sin r=(sin50^° / 1.5)
=(0.7660 / 1.5)=0.5107


Therefore,


r≈30.7^°


The ray bends towards the normal on entering the optically denser glass. Option C ignores refraction, while A and D incorrectly predict bending away from the normal.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: A ray incident normally on a plane surface
question: The incident ray coincides with the normal at the air–glass interface. A monochromatic ray is incident normally on a plane air–glass boundary. Which statement is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 88 H308" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" /><rect x="12" y="90" width="296" height="75" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M160 15 V154" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M153 26 L160 15 L167 26" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><path d="M160 90 V153" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="18" y="22" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="18" y="110" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Glass</text><text x="170" y="45" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal incidence</text></svg>

options.text: The ray bends towards the normal by an angle equal to the refractive index.
The ray bends away from the normal because glass is denser.
The ray passes undeviated, although its speed and wavelength decrease on entering glass.
The ray passes undeviated, and its speed, wavelength and frequency all remain unchanged.

explanation:
At normal incidence, i=0^°. Snell's law gives r=0^°, so the ray does not change direction. However,


v=(c / n)


and the wavelength decreases in glass, while frequency remains unchanged. Option D incorrectly assumes that no deviation means no change in optical properties.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Comparing incidence angle with the critical angle
question: A ray is incident from glass of refractive index 1.5 into air at 40^°. The critical angle for the glass–air interface is approximately 41.8^°. The incident ray makes an angle of 40^° with the normal. Which statement is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 180" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="8" y="90" width="304" height="78" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M8 90 H312 M160 15 V168" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M55 145 L160 90 L244 32" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M160 90 L244 32" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="18" y="110" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Glass</text><text x="18" y="20" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Air</text><text x="168" y="26" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text><text x="75" y="130" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">i = 40°</text><text x="220" y="24" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Refracted ray</text></svg>

options.text: Total internal reflection occurs because 40^° is close to the critical angle.
The ray is reflected completely because the incident medium is glass.
The refracted angle is 41.8^°.
The ray refracts into air at an angle greater than 40^°, but less than 90^°.

explanation:
Since 40^°<41.8^°, total internal reflection does not occur. By Snell's law,


1.5sin40^°=sin r



sin r≈0.9642


Therefore, r≈74.6^°, which is greater than 40^° but less than 90^°. Option A incorrectly assumes that being close to the critical angle is sufficient for total internal reflection.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Refraction through a prism versus a rectangular slab
question: Parallel slab Triangular prism The slab has parallel faces; the prism has non-parallel refracting faces. A ray passes obliquely through a rectangular glass slab and then through a triangular glass prism of the same material. Which difference is expected when both are surrounded by air and total internal reflection is absent?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 140 115" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="30" y="15" width="80" height="85" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" /><path d="M3 85 L30 64 L110 42 L137 21" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /><path d="M3 85 L30 64 L110 42 L137 21" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.2" fill="none" /></svg>

options.text: Both emergent rays must be parallel to their respective incident rays.
The slab produces angular deviation but no lateral displacement, whereas the prism produces neither.
The slab's emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray, whereas the prism generally produces an angular deviation because its refracting faces are not parallel.
The prism produces no refraction because the two faces have different orientations.

explanation: A parallel-sided slab produces equal and opposite angular changes at its two surfaces, leaving the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray but laterally displaced. A triangular prism has non-parallel refracting faces, so the deviations generally do not cancel. Option A incorrectly applies the slab result to a prism.

chapter: Refraction of Light at Plane Surfaces
title: Why an object seen through a plane glass window appears nearly in its true direction
question: The window has parallel faces, and the ray emerges into air on the opposite side. An object is viewed through a thin, parallel-sided glass window. Why is the apparent direction of the emergent ray the same as the direction of the incident ray, even though the ray bends inside the glass?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="120" y="15" width="80" height="145" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.22" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" /><path d="M10 130 L120 105 L200 91 L306 66" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M10 130 L306 66" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><text x="126" y="32" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Glass window</text><text x="14" y="146" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Object</text><text x="238" y="56" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Observer</text></svg>

options.text: The refractive index of glass is identical to that of air.
The second surface cancels the first surface's refraction because both surfaces are parallel, although a lateral displacement may remain.
The ray undergoes total internal reflection twice, restoring its original direction.
The ray bends towards the normal at both surfaces by equal angles.

explanation: The ray bends towards the normal on entering glass and away from the normal on leaving it. Parallel interfaces and the same external medium restore the original emergent direction. The emergent ray may still be laterally displaced. Option D is incorrect because the ray bends in opposite angular senses at the two interfaces.

title: Correct interpretation of a ray diagram for a transparent medium
question: The refracted ray makes a smaller angle with the normal than the incident ray. The ray diagram shows light entering medium Q from medium P and bending towards the normal. Which additional conclusion is valid, assuming the same frequency of light is maintained across the boundary?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 185" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 85 H310" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" /><rect x="10" y="87" width="300" height="82" fill="#60A5FA" fill-opacity="0.2" /><path d="M45 20 L160 85 L270 146" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M160 12 V170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-dasharray="4 4" stroke-width="1.1" /><text x="17" y="18" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Medium P</text><text x="17" y="105" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Medium Q</text><text x="173" y="25" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Normal</text><text x="205" y="137" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Ray in Q</text></svg>

options.text: The speed of light increases in Q, and the wavelength increases.
The frequency increases in Q, while the speed remains constant.
The speed decreases in Q, and the wavelength decreases.
The speed decreases in Q, but the wavelength increases.

explanation:
Bending towards the normal indicates entry into the optically denser medium for the given light. Thus the refractive index increases, and


v=(c / n)


decreases. Frequency remains unchanged, so lambda=v/f also decreases. Option D incorrectly predicts an increase in wavelength.

title: Advanced sunrise and delayed sunset
question: Starlight or sunlight bends progressively through atmospheric layers of varying refractive index. The Sun is geometrically just below the horizon, but the observer can still see its apparent image. Which explanation is correct?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 132 Q80 119 160 132 T312 132" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.2" fill="none" /><path d="M8 113 Q80 96 160 113 T312 113" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3" fill="none" /><path d="M8 92 Q80 75 160 92 T312 92" stroke="#64748B" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="4 3" fill="none" /><circle cx="254" cy="142" r="12" fill="#F59E0B" fill-opacity="0.8" /><path d="M254 142 L188 82 L105 47" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M105 47 L70 33" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2.5" fill="none" /><path d="M77 34 L70 33 L74 40" stroke="#D97706" stroke-width="2" fill="none" /><text x="12" y="20" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Observer</text><circle cx="30" cy="30" r="3" fill="currentColor" /><text x="207" y="169" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Geometric horizon</text><text x="17" y="151" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Earth</text><text x="12" y="72" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Atmosphere</text></svg>

options.text: Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight progressively towards regions of higher refractive index, making the Sun appear higher than its geometric position.
The atmosphere reflects all sunlight at the horizon by total internal reflection.
The Sun appears higher because the speed of light increases continuously as it enters denser atmospheric layers.
Atmospheric refraction changes the frequency of sunlight until it becomes visible above the horizon.

explanation:
is correct?

A) Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight progressively towards regions of higher refractive index, making the Sun appear higher than its geometric position.

B) The atmosphere reflects all sunlight at the horizon by total internal reflection.

C) The Sun appears higher because the speed of light increases continuously as it enters denser atmospheric layers.

D) Atmospheric refraction changes the frequency of sunlight until it becomes visible above the horizon.

**Correct Answer: A**

**Reason:**

Atmospheric density and refractive index generally increase closer to Earth's surface. Light curves through the atmosphere, and the backward extension of the final ray places the apparent Sun above its true geometric position. This causes advanced sunrise and delayed sunset. Option B incorrectly attributes the effect to total internal reflection.

question: A student plots sin i against sin r for light passing from air into glass. The graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient 1.5. What does the gradient represent?

options.text: The refractive index of glass relative to air.
The reciprocal of the refractive index of glass relative to air.
The speed of light in glass divided by the speed of light in air.
The critical angle of glass in degrees.

explanation:
Snell's law gives


n=(sin i / sin r)


The gradient of a graph of sin i against sin r is


(Δ(sin i) / Δ(sin r))=n=1.5


Option B would apply if the axes were interchanged. The gradient is a dimensionless ratio, not an angle.
